#7943. Four-Legged Surfers Make a Splash at International Surf Tournament

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Sayulita, on the coast of Nayarit, Mexico, is a dog-friendly surf town. Many pups spend their mornings with their paws in the sand while their owners head into the water to catch some waves. They dig the sand, run and play along the shore, and many sit patiently waiting for their parents to return. But, dogs being dogs, it's not hard to imagine how some of them have naturally followed their human right into the water to discover what the fun is all about.

For a surprising number of beach-going canines, surfing has become part of their world, and this year, the first dog-surfing contest in Sayulita took place as part of the International DÃ­a de Muertos Surf Tournament, held October 29 through November 1, 2026, at Playa Principal. Twelve dog-and-handler teams participated, making this a pawticularly special addition to the town's surf calendar. The main tournament, now in its third edition, brought together more than 120 athletes across several surfing disciplines.

The official program listed the dog category as an exhibition, with a prize pool of 10,000 Mexican pesos distributed among the top three. But for the pups, there was no question about the attraction: a surfboard, some waves, the chance to have fun with their favorite person, and a beach full of admirers? Paw me in!

Sayulita has been part of my life for a long time. As a teenager, I spent many weekends camping there, long before the main entrance road was paved or I imagined I would return as a veterinarian or spend time pet-sitting here.

In July and August this year, I looked after a wonderful rescue pup in Sayulita, and our daily walks took us along the main beach, past the local cemetery, for our daily swim in the beautiful Playa de los Muertos. It was a lovely way to experience the town beyond its busy surf beaches.

Sayulita is genuinely pet-friendly. Dogs are welcome on its beaches, and most restaurants accommodate four-legged visitors. They are part of the scenery, whether accompanying their pet parents through town or waiting patiently on the sand while someone catches a wave.

That makes the new dog-surfing event feel like a natural progression. Dogs have long been part of the local beach scene. This time, they got their own chance to take to the spotlight in the water.

The first Sayulita dog-surfing competition brought together 12 teams: Suleiman Navarro and Toto; Risa Mara Machuca and Chia; Lia Carbajal and Nita; Emiliano Cordova and Pelusa; Fernando Stalla and Miky; Carlos Rocha and Paddel; Eno James and Nemo; Nique Miller and Roy; Monse AcuÃ±a and Trinity; Luis Becerra and Knacki; Buzz Moro and LeÃ³n; and Kory De Jean and GÃ¼ero.

First place went to Suleiman Navarro and Toto, a blind Pug from Punta de Mita. Toto's visual impairment didn't keep him from joining the fun and riding the waves with Sule. Second place went to Fernando Stalla and Miky, who already enjoy surfing in Sayulita from time to time.

Risa Mara Machuca, known through @surfitoutmexico, helped bring the dog-surfing category to the event. Her own surfing partner, Chia, is already familiar with the sport beyond Sayulita. In August 2025, Chia and Risa became the first Mexican team to compete in the World Dog Surfing Competition in Pacifica, California.

Their surfing story began when Chia, who loved following Risa into the ocean, climbed onto a soft-top surfboard one day and headed straight for the front. Risa looked up at the sky and shouted, "Thank you, universe!"

It's hard not to appreciate a pup who discovers and genuinely enjoys a hobby shared with her favorite person. Chia's enthusiasm has helped give Sayulita a local connection to a sport attracting canine-human teams internationally.

My visit to Sayulita during DÃ­a de Muertos offered another glimpse into how much the community values their pups. The plaza and surrounding streets were specially decorated for the occasion. On the evening of November 1, we watched a procession leave the plaza as people gathered to honor loved ones who had passed away. Families continued the tradition of remembering the departed through decorations, flowers, and time spent together.

Many local establishments created traditional altars dedicated to their departed pets, with photographs and little tributes to beloved dogs included among the traditional decorations. It was lovely to see these four-legged family members remembered and celebrated as part of the town's DÃ­a de Muertos traditions.

October 27 has become a popular date in Mexico for remembering pets during the DÃ­a de Muertos season. Families may prepare small altars with photographs, favorite treats, toys, and water. This particular observance is a relatively recent popular custom rather than an ancient tradition followed everywhere, but it has found a meaningful place in many households.

Anyone who has loved and lost a dog can understand why. Pets become part of our daily routines, our families, and our memories. Seeing their photographs included in these celebrations gave me a lovely glimpse into the affection people in Sayulita have for their canine companions.

It also brought together two sides of the human-animal bond: remembering the dogs who are no longer with us while celebrating the ones still sharing our adventures.

Surfing isnât an activity for every dog, and thatâs okay. Like any activity, surfing should be reserved for dogs who voluntarily enjoy swimming and feel comfortable on a board. A well-fitted safety vest is always a good idea, like the cute one Chia wore, complete with its little shark fin! Not every dog is a water enthusiast, and that deserves just as much respect as celebrating the confident pups happy to take the spotlight. Waiting on the beach for their pet parents is a perfectly wonderful way to spend the day, too. As long as everyone is happy and the beach is left clean, that's a win for dogs and people alike.

Of course, the fun of watching dogs surf is only part of what made this event special. It also brought together two things that are so much a part of Sayulita: its surf culture and its affection for dogs.

The 2026 dog-surfing event added something genuinely new to the International DÃ­a de Muertos Surf Tournament. While the main competition celebrated its third year, the dogs were making their own history and adding to the unique charm of the event.

One of the nicest parts of returning to town was seeing how naturally dogs fit into both everyday life and local traditions. From the pups waiting patiently on the beach as their owners enjoy the waves, to the little altars honoring those who had passed away, there were reminders everywhere of the special place dogs hold in this community. Watching these dogs enjoy the waves alongside their pet parents was a lovely addition to a weekend already filled with celebration, music, and remembrance. Squirrels get a bad rep, but there's plenty of good reasons to want them in your garden (and not just because they're cute!).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You don't have to be a Disney princess to befriend a squirrel, which is good news for anyone who's long been keen to woo one of these cute critters themselves (ideally without a Snow White-level singsong).

Look, I'll level with you; I know that squirrels might not be everyone's favorite garden visitors. After all, they're notorious for raiding bird feeders, digging up freshly planted bulbs and burying nuts in flower pots. Before you declare war on these bushy-tailed garden acrobats, though, there's another side to consider... and not just the fact that they're the birth month animal for May babies everywhere.

Yes, squirrels can actually play a surprisingly useful role in the garden and wider ecosystem. From helping disperse tree seeds to spreading beneficial fungi, these busy little mammals contribute more to the natural world than you might realise. And they're also wonderfully entertaining to watch, with their energetic antics, impressive climbing skills and habit of darting between trees (so much so that it's well worth adding this charmingly rustic squirrel house to your backyard).

It's easy to focus on the damage squirrels can sometimes cause, but they also provide several ecological benefits. By digging and burying seeds, for example, they can help new trees and plants establish themselves, not to mention turn over small patches of soil.

Squirrels eat mushrooms and other fungi, helping disperse fungal spores which go on to form important relationships with tree roots, helping trees access nutrients and water. And let's not forget, either, that they are – sorry – an important food source for predators such as hawks, owls, foxes and other wildlife.

Rather than trying to keep squirrels out of your yard, why not consider making them feel welcome? With the right food, shelter and a little patience, you can encourage them to visit regularly and gradually become more comfortable with your presence.

Here's how to befriend a squirrel, then, along with some top tips on what to feed them and how to enjoy their company without sacrificing your bird feeders or flowers.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Squirrels are naturally drawn to gardens with plenty of trees, shrubs and places to hide. The easiest way to befriend a squirrel, then, is to offer up mature trees (which provide opportunities for climbing, nesting and foraging,) and dense shrubs that offer shelter from predators and bad weather.

Oak, hickory, beech and walnut trees are particularly valuable to many North American squirrel species because they produce nuts and seeds that provide natural food. So, if you have space, consider planting native trees and shrubs that offer food and shelter throughout the year.

One of the easiest ways to make your yard appealing to squirrels is to let nature do some of the work. Rather than removing every fallen nut, seed head or piece of natural debris, then, consider leaving a few areas where wildlife can forage.

Trees that produce acorns, walnuts and hickory nuts can provide valuable food, while berry-producing native shrubs offer additional opportunities for wildlife to feed. And you could also leave some fallen leaves in quieter areas of the garden, as these support insects and other small creatures that contribute to the wider ecosystem.

Anyone who's ever managed to befriend a squirrel before will tell you, in no uncertain terms, that offering small quantities of food always goes a long way!

Unsalted hazelnuts, walnuts and pecans in their shells provides a natural foraging activity. Sunflower seeds, too, are a familiar food source for many squirrel species, although they should only be offered in modest quantities. And plain pumpkin seeds can provide another occasional treat, too.

Natural food from your garden should always be the first port of call, of course; acorns, tree seeds and other naturally available foods are preferable to making squirrels dependent on a regular supply from you (especially as healthy wild squirrels don't really need supplementary feeding).

On that note, remember not to overfeed; the trick here is to only offer a small amount, remove uneaten food and avoid creating a feeding station that attracts large numbers of animals or unwanted pests. And take care to keep any feeding equipment clean, too, as communal feeding areas can allow diseases to spread between squirrels.

Like other wildlife, squirrels need access to fresh water, and a shallow birdbath or a wildlife water dish like this one can provide a convenient drinking spot, particularly during hotter, drier weather.

Just as you would for your beloved birds, make sure the water is kept clean and refreshed regularly. Adding a few stones can also provide a helpful foothold for smaller creatures, too, and don't forget to position the water somewhere squirrels can reach safely (ideally near trees or shrubs that offer a quick escape route).

Perhaps the most rewarding part of welcoming squirrels into your garden is watching them gradually become more comfortable with your presence. Start by simply observing them from a distance, and then try to spend a little time in the garden without making sudden movements or approaching them.

If you provide a small amount of food, use the same designated feeding area and let squirrels discover it independently. Over time, they may become accustomed to seeing you in the garden and feel more comfortable foraging while you're nearby.

Even if you are attempting to befriend a squirrel, please don't attempt to chase, touch or hand-feed them. Even seemingly friendly squirrels can bite or scratch if they feel threatened, and encouraging wildlife to approach people can create problems for both animals and humans.

If you want to welcome squirrels without losing your bird feeders, consider using squirrel-resistant feeders, particularly models with weight-activated mechanisms that close feeding ports when a heavier animal climbs aboard.

You can also install a squirrel baffle on feeder poles to prevent squirrels from climbing up to reach the food. And don't forget to position feeders away from nearby trees, fences and other launching points wherever possible, as squirrels are surprisingly good at jumping.

If you'd like to provide food for both birds and squirrels, consider giving them separate feeding areas. This can help reduce competition, although it won't guarantee that squirrels won't investigate the bird feeders.

If you want to stop squirrels digging up your flower bulbs, be sure to protect the plants you want to keep safe. This might mean covering newly planted bulbs with wire mesh or use protective bulb baskets, as these allow plants to grow while making it much harder for squirrels to reach the bulbs.

Alternatively, you can also cover the soil in containers with suitable mesh or another physical barrier, particularly during the autumn planting season. This approach allows squirrels to continue visiting the garden while protecting the areas where their digging is less welcome.

Squirrels might occasionally test a gardener's patience, but they're also fascinating little creatures that play a role in supporting healthy ecosystems.

If you want to befriend a squirrel, you may find that simply providing natural food sources, shelter and fresh water does the trick! And if you do decide to put out the occasional treat, remember that moderation and good hygiene are important; these are wild animals, and the aim should be to encourage natural visits rather than turn them into pets.

Oh sure, you might not be able to stop every squirrel from investigating your bird feeders or digging in your flower beds, but learning to accommodate these lively visitors? Well, that could make your garden a much more interesting place to spend time in the long run...

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#7941. The Most Common Fatal Diseases in Cats, and How to Avoid Them

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

Lowering the risk: Genetics play a big part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which shows up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

Lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

This is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight quickly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

Up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

Lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

Rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

Lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

Lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a plan for each cat.

#7940. Bored, Overtired, or Just Being a Dog? What Makes Puppies Hyper

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

The opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

Puppies learn quickly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

All puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

Food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and new situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

Most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health issues is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

Puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

Most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

Researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

Activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

Most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health issues. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

#7939. From Cat-astrophe to Cat-tastic: The Story of Snickers the Smiling Cat

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Snickers is a calico cat born in Owensboro, Kentucky, USA, whose adorable âsmileâ has hundreds of thousands of fans. Her life journey hasnât always been smooth, but this remarkable cat touches the heart of every person she meets along the way. It was her fierce personality that inspired her pawrent, Kelly DeWeese, to go to great lengths to ensure Snickers gets to live her best life.

June 2020 was a challenging time for Kelly. She had recently lost her mother, leaving her in a state of grief, and in an attempt to find solace and cope with her loss, she took up running. It was during one of these runs, only her second, that a tiny, fragile kitten crossed her path.

Kelly was jogging past vast cornfields, and her mind was hyper-focused on the pleasing sound of the stalks rustling in the wind when a small calico kitten appeared out of the blue. She was alone, sick, and desperately in need of help.

Snickers, as she would later be christened, was in terrible shape. Her eyes were crusted shut; she couldn't meow, and she had severe respiratory issues, including sneezing. Her frail body was covered in fleas, and it was clear she was suffering.

Moved by compassion, Kelly scooped up the little kitten and carried her the two miles back to her home, where she was given a much-needed bath and plenty of TLC. The following day, Kelly took her to the local veterinarian, who ran various tests and initiated a series of treatments.

Despite the efforts of the local vet, the situation didn't improve, and the bills were mounting. Snickers' condition was dire.

Despite the financial strain, Kelly's determination to save Snickers was unwavering. After several trips to the vet, it became clear that this brave little kitten needed specialized care. Snickers was referred to a specialist in Louisville, Kentucky, two hours away. There, a CT scan revealed the root of her health issues: large polyps behind her eyes and deep within her inner ear.

The specialist recommended two major surgeries to remove the polyps. The surgeries were spaced six weeks apart and were extremely expensive. The first surgery was a great success, but the second operation had a life-altering consequence. During the procedure, one of the polyps slipped into her neck, temporarily cutting off oxygen to the brain. She essentially died for a few seconds before the surgical team managed to resuscitate her with CPR. Tragically, Snickers woke up from the operation blind.

The prognosis was uncertain, with a 50/50 chance of her regaining her eyesight. But Kelly, determined and resolute, refused to give up on her beloved feline companion. She watched over Snickers as she adjusted to her newfound blindness, never losing hope.

Remarkably, a couple of months later, a miracle occurred. One day, while she was waving something in front of Snickers, the catâs reaction gave Kelly a glimmer of hope. It appeared that Snickers might be regaining her eyesight. Ecstatic about this newfound possibility, Kelly promptly took Snickers back to the specialist, who confirmed the miraculous news: Snickers had indeed regained her eyesight.

Now, Snickers is a thriving and healthy six-year-old cat, bearing her distinctive, always-smiling face. Her remarkable journey from a sickly, abandoned kitten to a joyful, beloved family member is a testament to the power of love and determination. Her infectious smile serves as a constant reminder that sometimes, in the face of adversity, the most extraordinary things can happen. Kelly's unyielding commitment to Snickers proves that every life, no matter how small, is worth fighting for.

All those present at the veterinary clinic will agree that Snickers' recovery was nothing short of a miracle, and her journey to health and happiness continued to inspire those who heard her story. Kelly, who had been enduring a challenging period in her life when she found Snickers, felt that the little calico had rescued her just as much as she had rescued the cat. Their bond deepened as they supported each other through adversity.

As Snickers regained her eyesight and settled into her new, loving home, it was increasingly evident that she was not your typical feisty calico. Her sweet and calm disposition was a stark contrast to the naughty tortie stereotype, with endearing quirks that set her apart, such as sitting with a posture that resembled a human's. Snickers took an interest in watching television and enjoyed playing fetch, showcasing her unique personality.

Her joyful demeanor and cheerful, almost constant smile brought a special kind of happiness to Kelly's life. She couldn't help but feel that Snickers was fully aware of her love. The little calico has found her forever home and is living her best life.

Snickers' story didn't end with her recovery. She quickly became a star on Kelly's Instagram, captivating her followers with the charming and humorous poses she struck. Snickers has an uncanny ability to assume positions that make it appear as though she were a human in a cat's body. She gazes intently at the camera as if she knew she was a star.

Not only does Snickers sport a perpetual smile on her face, but she also has a surprise waiting on one of her pawsâa smiley face marking. This unique and heartwarming feature only adds to her charm.

Kelly's devotion to Snickers, both emotionally and financially, is unwavering. She recognizes that many people might not have been willing to invest the considerable amount she did to save a sick kitten, especially one that had a grim prognosis. Many might have chosen to take the easier path and euthanize the cat.

Yet Kelly saw past the hardships and the steep financial costs. Snickers had been loving and sweet from the moment she entered Kelly's life, and Kelly simply couldn't give up on her. The life insurance money she had received after her mother's passing became a lifeline for Snickers, a way to provide the specialized care and surgeries that ultimately saved her life.

For Kelly, the choice to sacrifice a significant portion of her savings was clear. She believed it was a way to honor her mother's memory by making a difference in the life of a helpless creature. Money became secondary in the face of compassion and determination, and over $10K in donations from the public showed how generous people can be when they see someone in need of support.

Snickers and Kelly's story is a testament to the extraordinary transformations that can occur when we refuse to give up, even in the face of daunting challenges. Snickers, with her perpetual smiling face and smiley paw, embodies the spirit of resilience and the profound impact that love and dedication can have on a life, no matter how small or furry.

Their story continues to serve as a beacon of hope and a reminder that sometimes, in the most unexpected moments, we find our greatest sources of joy and inspiration.

Originally from San Diegoâs sunshine and now living amongst Kentuckyâs rolling hills, I've built a cozy life powered by cat love and everyday warmth. I'm the kind of person who turns simple moments into little rituals, especially with my favorite feline co-star, Snickers.

As temperatures dip and the nights draw in, why not look to your birth month winter bird to learn more about your personality?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The seasons are shifting, which means our feathered friends are about to embark upon a changing of the guard... so which is your birth month winter bird, you ask?

It's not a silly question, by any means. After all, some birds migrate south for winter, some arrive from further north, and year-round residents shift their habits. And, from the brilliant red cardinal perched against a snowy backdrop to the tiny dark-eyed junco hopping beneath a bird feeder, these seasonal visitors have plenty of personality.

With that in mind, then, what if every month had its own winter bird to call its own? What might it reveal about the people born under its wings?

Now, we’re already familiar with the idea of a classic birth month bird, not to mention the birth month owl and birth month bird of prey, but what might the unique traits that make each winter bird so wonderful say about our own personalities?

Some are bold and charismatic, others are quiet and contemplative, and a few are wonderfully independent. All, though, are beautiful in their own special way, and so much fun to watch as they go about their business over the colder months.

With that in mind, then, I've paired 12 fascinating winter birds with the personality traits commonly associated with each birth month, along with a few easy ways you can make your garden a more welcoming place for them. Time to grab yourself a motion-activated wildlife camera with night vision, like the GardePro on Amazon, then, and start reading...

And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then enter our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you're born in January, you're likely to be headstrong, disciplined and hardworking (all of which are, natural leadership qualities, just in case you fancied informing your boss). Naturally, then, your birth month winter bird is a wonderful reflection of that determination: the snow bunting.

These beautiful little birds are highly social during winter, often gathering in flocks to forage for seeds in open fields and along shorelines, while their ability to thrive in bitterly cold conditions is rather impressive for such a small bird.

Like January babies, basically, they don't shy away from a challenge; they meet it head-on! To help them do this, be sure to leave native grasses and seed-producing plants standing where possible, rather than tidying every corner of your garden.

One of the most iconic birds in the world, the striking snowy owl has brilliant white plumage, piercing yellow eyes and an unmistakable presence. They spend much of the year in the Arctic, but some travel south during winter, occasionally appearing in northern parts of the United States (although they tend to favour wide-open landscapes, including coastal dunes, fields and other exposed areas where they can hunt).

Often solitary hunters, February's birth month winter bird gets by on its own instincts and remarkable ability to spot prey from a distance. It's also wonderfully adapted to its harsh environment, making it a fitting symbol of independence, deep-thinking, and inner strength.

To help snowy owls out over the colder months, avoid using rodenticides that can poison birds of prey, turn your garden into an owl hangout (it only takes five plants), and always give any owl you encounter plenty of space.

March babies are often associated with introspection, creativity, compassion and a thoughtful nature. It makes a whole lot of sense, then, that their birth month winter bird is the dark-eyed junco, a small but charming visitor that brings plenty of life to colder gardens.

Sometimes nicknamed the snowbird, dark-eyed juncos tend to spend much of their time quietly hopping around on the ground, searching for fallen seeds beneath trees and feeders. As such, they're a lovely match for March personalities: observant, gentle and happy to enjoy the quieter things in life.

If you fancy seeing more in your garden, remember that juncos are particularly fond of feeding on the ground, so provide a sheltered feeding area with small seeds. Leaving native grasses and seed heads standing also gives them more natural foraging opportunities.

If you're an April baby, you're thought to be charismatic, energetic, straightforward and naturally confident. As such, there's perhaps no better bird to represent you than the unmistakable blue jay.

With its brilliant blue plumage, distinctive crest and loud calls, the blue jay certainly knows how to make itself noticed. These intelligent members of the crow family have bold personalities that often make them one of the most entertaining birds to watch, in fact.

Blue jays are also clever problem-solvers, not to mention never afraid to make their presence known. Plant native oak trees and other nut-producing species to provide natural food and shelter to help them out, and remember that they also enjoy unsalted peanuts , so you can occasionally offer some in a suitable feeder.

I know, I know; a wild turkey might not feel like the most glamorous birth month winter bird, but hear me out! May personalities are often described as sociable, talented, loyal and strong-willed. And wild turkeys? Why, they're highly social, often gathering in flocks during winter as they search for food, not to mention putting on some impressive courtship displays.

They're also resourceful foragers, searching through woodland floors for seeds, nuts, berries and insects. During colder months, they can be spotted scratching through leaf litter and searching beneath trees for whatever food they can find. To help yours out, then, take care to leave natural cover in place where possible, and avoid using pesticides that reduce the insects and other natural food sources they rely on.

Known for its melancholy-sounding coo, the gentle mourning dove is a familiar sight across much of the United States, often seen perched on telephone wires, fences and tree branches, or quietly searching the ground for seeds.

They're also known for their strong pair bonds, with partners often working together to raise their young, so it's easy to see why this bird suits June babies (especially as they tend to be such romantic dreamers). It's a birth month winter bird that perfectly aligns with all of that sensitivity and imagination.

Remember, mourning doves enjoy feeding on the ground, so provide a clean feeding area with something like sunflower hearts if you want to see them in your garden. Plant some native seed-producing plants and shrubs, too, to help provide natural food and shelter.

July babies are adventurous free spirits known for their cheerful and (ahem) slightly slightly eccentric personalities, not to mention their strong protective streaks when it comes to family. It was inevitable, then, that the snow goose would prove their birth month winter bird.

Known for their impressive journeys between breeding and wintering grounds, snow geese are often spotted travelling in enormous flocks that fill the sky with their distinctive calls. They are also strongly connected to family life; young birds travel with their parents, and family groups can remain together during migration and winter.

If you want to help your feathery soulmate out, remember that snow geese depend on healthy wetlands, grasslands and agricultural landscapes during migration and winter. Supporting wetland conservation and protecting natural resting and feeding areas, then, is one of the best ways to keeo them thriving.

It makes so much sense that August babies get the delightful red-breasted nuthatch as their birth month winter bird, as it sums up all their best qualities perfectly. Yes, this little bird might be small, but it certainly doesn't lack confidence. One of its most entertaining habits is climbing headfirst down tree trunks, something it does with remarkable ease as it searches for insects and seeds hidden in the bark.

During autumn and winter, red-breasted nuthatches also collect and store conifer seeds, helping ensure they have food available when conditions become more challenging. They're hardworking, resourceful and rather determined, making them a lovely match for August birthdays.

To help them out, try to plant native trees such as pine, spruce and fir where appropriate for your region. You can also offer sunflower seeds, peanuts or suet in a clean feeder, particularly during colder weather.

Intelligent, spiritual, organized and analytical, September babies tend to be more successful in life (genuinely; look it up!) and thus are represented by the pine siskin.

These small finches might be easy to overlook at first, but they're fascinating little birds. They are adaptable, clever, and brimming with plenty of resourcefulness, though, which is why you often seen clinging to the tips of pine branches and even hanging upside down as they extract seeds from cones.

Sure, they're rather unpredictable visitors, as their movements depend heavily on food availability; this means that some gardens might welcome large flocks one winter and see very few the next. To keep them flocking, grow native conifers and other seed-producing plants to provide natural food, as well as nyjer (thistle) seed and sunflower hearts in finch feeders.

As an October baby myself, I'm more than happy to see this charming wanderer as my birth month winter bird! Especially as, with its striking yellow, black and white plumage and enormous pale bill, this chunky finch is one of North America's most distinctive birds.

Evening grosbeaks are adventurous travellers, sometimes moving considerable distances in search of food during autumn and winter. They're also wonderfully sociable, often gathering in groups around food sources and making quite an impression when they arrive at a backyard feeder.

For October birthdays, they're a lovely symbol of persistence, confidence and a little good fortune. After all, spotting one can feel like winning a small birdwatching lottery (although you can boost your chances with a handful of black-oil sunflower seeds, which can be offered in a sturdy platform feeder).

Empathetic, generous, brave and deeply determined, November-born souls are represented by one of North America's most magnificent waterbirds: the trumpeter swan.

These enormous white swans are impressive in every sense, with long necks, powerful wings and a distinctive black bill. They are known for their strong pair bonds and devoted parenting, and their family groups can be particularly striking to see gliding across a winter lake. In fact, it's their loyalty, protective instincts and graceful strength that make them a beautiful match for November birthdays.

These aren't traditional garden birds, so you can help them by protecting local wetlands, ponds and freshwater habitats, and always taking care to avoid disturbing swans when they're resting or feeding.

Generous, patriotic, optimistic and willing to take a few risks? Yeah, obviously the birth month winter bird for December is the cardinal!

Known for their strong pair bonds and the way they communicate through a variety of musical calls, their cheerful appearance against bare branches and snowy gardens has led to them becoming something not unlike a symbol of hope during the festive season. In fact, many believe that if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st, you're owed 12 months of love, optimism, and luck for the year ahead.

If you want to help yours out, plant native berry-producing shrubs such as winterberry, serviceberry and dogwood to make your garden a one-stop destination for food, shelter, and nesting opportunities.

Whether you believe in the concept of a birth month winter bird or not, there's no denying that they serve as a lovely reminder of just how much wildlife is around us, even during the coldest months of the year.

And perhaps the best part is that you don't have to wait for your own birth month to enjoy these feathered visitors. By planting native trees and shrubs, leaving seed heads standing, providing clean water and maintaining safe feeding areas, you can help make your garden a welcoming winter refuge for your feathered friends throughout the year.

Give it a go, I say! You'll do your bit for local wildlife and you might even discover a new favorite feathered friend along the way...

#7937. War Dogs of History: Chips

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, New York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

Chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

Chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, quickly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the company commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

In 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

Washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

In January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

Chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

Morgan Farr is a writer, graphic designer, and advocate who has spent her career telling the stories of working dogs and the people who love them. She serves as the Social Media Coordinator for both the Military Working Dog Heritage Museum and the National Service Animals Monument. She previously served as the social media manager for the U.S. Army Military Working Dog Program.

Together with her husband, an Army veterinarian, Morgan co-founded Canine Advancement Group, which offers education on canine wellness and welfare for both working and companion dogs. She is a member of the American Veterinary Medical History Society, the American Historical Association, the American Association for State and Local History, and the Society for Military History. In 2025, she was named the Armed Forces Insurance Military Spouse of the Year for Joint Base San Antonio.

At home, Morgan is a military spouse, a homeschooling mother of four, a small business owner of Dog-Eared Press, and a co-op instructor. She shares her household with a high-drive Dutch Shepherd and a spirited Bombay cat, who remind her daily that every animal, working or companion, deserves understanding, partnership, and thoughtful care.

After dazzling us with their fiery fall foliage, Japanese maples deserve a little TLC to help them weather winter and return in all their glory next year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage. It's my little jewel of the garden, a sentiment shared by many of my friends with these small trees in their landscapes.

Japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage. Since these trees are usually hardy down to USDA zone 4 or 5, they may shrug off winter cold. But that doesn’t make them immune to winter damage from the cold weather, harsh winds, and fluctuating soil moisture. Young trees and container trees are especially vulnerable.

So you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter. If not, you’ve come to the right place. This guide explains the six simple but essential tasks to ensure your Japanese maple makes it through winter with flying colors. You can do them at the same time as your other garden winterizing tasks.

Don’t worry too much about watering your Japanese maple during winter. When the leaves fall and the tree enters dormancy, it needs very little water. Water trees only if there has been no precipitation for several weeks and the ground is bone dry.

However, to help them through the winter, give them one final irrigation before the ground freezes. If the summer has been hot and/or dry, make this a deep watering. A soaker hose is ideal for delivering a slow, even soaking across the tree's root zone without wasting water. The Gilmour Round Soaker Hose from Amazon is a good option, as it distributes water evenly along its length.

Tuck a cozy blanket of mulch around your precious tree in November. Use something organic – wood chips or bark work well. Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot is a good option, made from natural, shredded wood. Layer up to 4 inches (10 cm) of mulch over the root zone. This protects the roots, holds heat in the soil, and prevents frost heaving.

Don’t make the mistake of piling the mulch up against the trunk in a “volcano” arrangement. The mulch should never touch the trunk since that can cause wood rot.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Is your Japanese maple a young tree you planted within the last three years? You’ll want to give the juvenile tree extra protection. This will also be true if you live in a region with an exceptionally cold winter.

In these circumstances, help your tree survive with insulation. Wrap vulnerable trunks or branches with burlap, such as this Riare Natural Burlap Plant Protection Wrap from Amazon, to shield them against harsh, drying winter winds. Leave the burlap loose enough to allow the tree to breathe.

If your tree has broken or diseased branches, the best time to take those off is now, whenever you notice. And you should check regularly to spot problems early. But aside from this type of damage, do not give your Japanese maple a haircut in November or at any other point during dormancy. Pruning at this time can leave cuts vulnerable to disease and frost damage.

Would you have an energy drink just before bedtime? Of course not. And for all the same reasons, do not fertilize your Japanese maple in November. Fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, induces new growth just as the tree should be entering winter dormancy. This new growth is tender and will easily freeze in the first flush of winter weather, leading to dieback or split bark.

In spring, if your tree needs feeding, use a gentle, slow-release fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Tree-tone (6-3-2) from Amazon. Apply sparingly, following the package instructions, as Japanese maples generally don't need much fertilizer.

It won’t surprise you to hear that container maple trees require more protection than a Japanese maple with its roots deep in the garden soil. Their roots are much closer to the cold air on all sides, and therefore can freeze or dry out faster.

You’ll want to take steps to protect a potted Japanese maple. A good first step is to insulate the containers with bubble wrap or burlap. Wrap the pots well and cluster the containers together near the house to attract radiant heat. It also helps to use pot feet, like Bosmere's Pot Toes, or even wood blocks to raise the containers off the cold ground and support good drainage.

In the most severe winters, you can move your container trees into a shelter, like an unheated garage or a sheltered porch.

Does your tree still have leaves as Thanksgiving arrives? This is normal, not a cause for alarm.

Trees have an abscission layer at the base of their leaf stems that releases the leaves to fall in the cold. But Japanese maples build this layer more slowly than other deciduous trees like red or sugar maples. And if you’ve had a mild autumn, this can delay leaf drop even further, even into December.

This means additional watering work for you. While your maple still has leaves, you’ll need to keep watering whenever the soil is dry. At the same time, rake up leaves that do fall and remove them. You don’t want soggy or decaying piles of maple leaves since this can encourage the spread of fungal spores.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7934. Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v. Yip, joined by Justice Alito (Justice Gorsuch voted to grant the petition, but didn't sign on to the dissent):

In 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes. The Ninth Circuit held that First Amendment scrutiny did not apply to this compelled-speech requirement because the breadth of California's CME regulation renders the content of any CME course government speech, not private speech. That logic fundamentally misunderstands this Court's precedents and the Constitution. First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.

I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine. At a minimum, the Ninth Circuit misapplied Shurtleff v. Boston (2022), which instructs courts to identify government speech by considering (1) "the history of the expression at issue," (2) "the public's likely perception as to who (the government or a private person) is speaking," and (3) "the extent to which the government has actively shaped or controlled the expression." The Ninth Circuit collapsed those distinct inquiries, focusing on the breadth of the government's regulatory scheme at each step. More fundamentally, however, Shurtleff is leading courts astray.

I joined Justice ALITO's concurrence in Shurtleff, which warned that the majority's three-factor test could cause courts to conclude that extensive government regulation transforms a private message into government speech exempt from First Amendment scrutiny. As the Ninth Circuit's decision shows, those concerns were prescient. This Court should reconsider whether the Shurtleff test is the proper mode of analysis for identifying government speech…

California-licensed physicians are required to complete 50 hours of approved CME every two years. Credit-eligible CME courses are often organized by private entities, certified by private accreditors, and taught by private instructors. The State does not preapprove course content but reserves the right to audit courses for compliance with its CME standards.

The Medical Board of California "adopt[s] and administer[s] [CME] standards," few of which relate to course content. In addition, the State requires that CME courses broadly relate to the medical profession. They must "serve to maintain, develop, or increase the knowledge, skills, and professional performance that a physician and surgeon uses to provide care, or to improve the quality of care provided to patients." In 2019, however, the California Legislature added a requirement that after January 1, 2022, all CME courses must "contain curriculum that includes the understanding of implicit bias." To satisfy that requirement, CME courses must contain "[e]xamples of how implicit bias affects perceptions and treatment decisions of physicians and surgeons, leading to disparities in health outcomes" or "[s]trategies to address how unintended biases in decisionmaking may contribute to health care disparities."

Petitioners Dr. Azadeh Khatibi and Do No Harm do not want to speak California's preferred message on implicit bias, and they challenged § 2190.1(d) as compelling speech in violation of the First Amendment. Dr. Khatibi, a California-licensed ophthalmologist, creates and teaches CME courses. She "disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in healthcare" and does not want to devote time to the subject during her courses. Do No Harm is a nonprofit corporation. At least one of its members teaches CME courses and believes that implicit bias trainings "have not been shown to successfully reduce barriers to healthcare, and instead risk infecting healthcare decisions with divisive and discriminatory ideas." Yet, California's implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State's view that implicit bias causes "disparities in health outcomes…..

The Ninth Circuit held that all three Shurtleff factors indicate that "CMEs eligible for Board credit constitute government speech." At every step of the analysis, the Ninth Circuit emphasized the breadth of the State's regulation. Considering history, the court noted that California "has long regulated the practice of medicine as an exercise of the police power" and has "adopted, updated, and enforced CME standards." Considering the public's likely perception of the speaker in a CME course, the court reasoned that "licensees could attribute approved CMEs' content to California" because "their profession is heavily regulated." Considering the extent to which the government has shaped the expression, the court cited "California's extraordinary control over accredited CMEs." As Judge VanDyke explained in his dissent from the denial of rehearing en banc, the panel's "approach boil[ed] down to a single-factor analysis: does the government 'heavily' or 'actively' regulate CMEs?" …

In its blinkered application of the Shurtleff factors, the Ninth Circuit lost sight of the core government-speech inquiry: whether the government is "speak[ing] for itself or … regulat[ing] private expression."

The government-speech doctrine occupies a narrow corner of our First Amendment jurisprudence. The First Amendment protects the people's right of free speech against government interference; it does not prevent the government from speaking for itself. "But courts must be very careful when a government claims that speech by one or more private speakers is actually government speech." "If private speech could be passed off as government speech by simply affixing a government seal of approval, government could … muffle the expression of disfavored viewpoints," or, as here, require private speakers to convey government messages without facing any constitutional scrutiny.

This Court has thus exercised "great caution" before characterizing a message as government speech. In Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Assn (2005), we held that government-sponsored beef ads constituted government speech because the government determined "the overarching message" of the ads, helped develop proposals for the ads, reviewed every ad "for substance and for wording," and the Secretary of Agriculture "exercise[d] final approval authority over every word used in every" ad. In Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009), we held that the permanent display of monuments in a public park was government speech because the City "effectively controlled the messages sent by the monuments in the Park by exercising final approval authority over their selection." And, in Walker v. Texas Div., Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc. (2015), we held that the messages on government-issued license plates, over which the State "maintain[ed] direct control," were government speech.

Since Walker—which we have described as the "outer boun[d] of the government-speech doctrine," Matal v. Tam (2017)—we have been careful to distinguish between government control over messages and government control over the broader scheme through which the messages are communicated. We held, for example, that trademarks are private speech, notwithstanding the government's substantial involvement in the registration process. And, this Court held that flags flown outside of Boston's City Hall did not constitute government speech in part because the city regularly permitted private groups to freely fly their own colors. In all these cases, the controlling question was whether "the government intends to speak for itself or to regulate private expression."

Put in those simple terms, and in light of our precedents, California's attempt to require private individuals in privately accredited CME courses to run implicit-bias training is an evident attempt "to regulate private expression." … First, California has not historically used CME to communicate government messages. While the State requires that CME courses generally relate to the practice of medicine and occasionally requires that courses cover certain subjects, California has not otherwise dictated the content of courses.

Second, because California "relie[s] on the participation of private parties in executing the CME scheme," the public is unlikely to perceive a private instructor's CME course as government speech. As the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, Dr. Khatibi "plausibly alleged facts suggesting that attendees treat her as the person responsible for CME content."

Third, while California extensively regulates the medical field, licenses physicians, and sets the requirements for credit-eligible CME, there is little evidence that California "shape[s] the messages" communicated in CME courses. Despite its long recitation of California regulations, the Ninth Circuit did not identify any state law that requires private speakers in a CME course to express a particular viewpoint—even on contestable medical issues. The implicit-bias-training requirement is a notable departure from that practice. It should have been easy, then, for the courts below to conclude that California's implicit-bias-training requirement regulates private speech.

More troubling than the Ninth Circuit's misapplication of the Shurtleff factors are the implications of the court's decision. On the Ninth Circuit's view of government speech, could California require a CME instructor to communicate the State's preferred message on the availability of abortion? Could the State require a CME instructor to inform participants that for certain patients, gender-transition surgery is ethically required?

What of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring? Applying the Ninth Circuit's logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker's message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court's precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution….

If the Ninth Circuit's decision is truly the kind of result that Shurtleff's three-factor test countenances, we should reconsider Shurtleff. Before Shurtleff, this Court had identified history, public perception, and government control as "relevant" but not mandatory "considerations" for identifying government speech. When Shurtleff described those considerations as a three-factor test, several Members of the Court—myself included—warned that the test would be unworkable and obscure the central inquiry in government-speech cases: whether the government is speaking or regulating private speech. "[L]ike any factorized analysis," the Shurtleff majority's approach does not "provide a principled way of deciding cases." Worse, myopic focus on the history and scope of government control over speech may give courts the false impression that state regulation can convert private speech into government speech.

After only a few years, those concerns are materializing. The Ninth Circuit relied on California's regulation of CME to conclude that requiring private speakers to communicate a government message was not compelled speech but government speech. That is precisely the paradox predicted by the concurrence in Shurtleff: that "government action that regulates private speech would" now "qualify as government speech unregulated by the First Amendment." But, neither compelled speech nor "[c]ensorship" are "made constitutional by aggressive and direct application." It cannot be the case that compelled speech becomes government speech because the government has compelled the speech.

I would grant certiorari to correct course. In my view, the relevant inquiry in a government-speech case is straightforward: Is the government "speaking," or is it "regulating private expression"? The challenged government activity must be "government speech in the literal sense—purposeful communication of a governmentally determined message by a person acting within the scope of a power to speak for the government." Moreover, "the government must … not rely on a means that abridges the speech of persons acting in a private capacity," because doing so reveals that the government has moved from the role of speaker to that of regulator.

Under this framework, it is easy to see why California's law is subject to First Amendment scrutiny. The State's implicit-bias-training requirement is not speech by any government actor; it is a requirement that private speakers communicate certain messages. Although the government may "deputiz[e] private persons as its agents" to convey its message, Dr. Khatibi and Do No Harm's members have not "voluntarily assumed" "a public or quasi-public capacity that empowers them to speak on behalf of the government." They share their own messages through the CME courses they create and deliver, and they do so in their private capacities. Even "government speech in the literal sense is not exempt from First Amendment attack if it uses a means that restricts private expression," such as "compelled speech." When, as here, the government does not issue its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government's viewpoint, the First Amendment applies….

A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as "a cover for censorship" or a cloak for compelled speech.

NEXT: Washington May Permit Nudity-Focused Businesses "to Set Entry Requirements Based on Genitalia"

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.
