Your garden beds may be looking tired, but there's no need for back-breaking work. Just four simple layers can help replenish them in time for spring planting.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task. Some of us gardeners love planting flowers but don’t enjoy raking leaves. Others like tucking mulch around their shrubs but won’t pull weeds. But digging up the garden dirt and turning it over is not high on anyone’s list of favorite tasks.

So just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening. It’s a clever, no-dig technique that works best in fall. Leave the shovel in the garage and instead, stack layers of cardboard, fallen leaves, and other organic materials over the garden soil, letting them break down naturally over winter. The result is fertile planting beds for spring.

Ready to get “cooking”? Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.

Of course you love your garden, but wouldn’t it be nice if the garden could do most of the work of preparing the beds for spring planting? Lasagna gardening, aka no-dig or no-till gardening, allows your garden to do most of the work of decomposition and replenishment. The technique is really cold composting in place.

This low-effort process works like home composting: alternate layers of green and brown materials, then let them break down into the soil. Cut grass and kitchen scraps are green materials; cardboard and dried leaves are brown materials. Your “lasagna” is a compost heap waiting to happen.

You can also think of lasagna gardening as mimicking the forest floor. It works the same way soil is built up in a woodland. First, leaves pile up and decompose on the forest floor. Along come microbes and worms that transform that debris into rich soil. Lasagna gardening follows the same pattern, making your garden bed into a soil ecosystem.

When you make a lasagna for dinner, you just layer up the pasta, the ragù, the sauce, and grated cheese, then pop it in the oven. Without any additional work on your part, a luscious dinner will be ready when it is time to eat.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A winter lasagna garden uses the same system. You stack up four layers, then leave it to decompose. Without any additional work on your part, your garden will have rich, fertile soil for spring. Here are the four key layers.

Think of cardboard as the weed barrier. First, weed-whack or mow the area to cut down any weeds or grass. A cordless string trimmer, like this Worx model, makes things easier.

Then, lay sheets of flattened cardboard right over the soil in your garden, using overlapping layers to cover the entire area. Heavy, corrugated cardboard works best to keep grass and weeds out while still welcoming earthworms. After that is done, douse all of the cardboard with lukewarm water.

This is the carbon layer, supporting soil microbes and providing structural aeration. I like using dry autumn leaves (what else are you going to do with them?), but a thick layer of any type of brown material will work, giving your garden soil a carbon-rich environment. Alternatives include straw, peat moss, sawdust, wood chips, or shredded newspaper.

If you don't have enough waste materials to hand, a bag of garden straw mulch, like this HealthiStraw GardenStraw from Walmart, is an easy way to bulk up this layer.

Here’s the “compost” element of the lasagna. Your green materials will be in charge of making the garden soil a nitrogen-rich environment that heats up and fuels the decay process. Together with the brown material, they make the garden one giant compost pile. You can use kitchen waste, but also toss in some grass clippings, coffee grounds, or even manure.

If you can't source enough green material for free, then pick up a bag of composted cow manure, such as Black Kow, available at Home Depot.

You aren’t limited to one layer of brown material and one layer of green. Keep right on stacking alternating layers, using about twice as much brown as green. Two, three, or even four alternating layers of organic material can speed things up for your garden bed.

Flattened cardboard lays the foundation for the lasagna; compost or topsoil serves as a top cap. For a ready-made option, try Back to the Roots Organic Compost from Home Depot. This is especially important if you are planning on planting immediately. This rich layer is at the top of the pile so that your seeds will have what it takes to establish strong roots in short order.

A lasagna garden is an attractive option if low-maintenance is a priority. Once you create your lasagna, wonderful things begin to happen and keep on happening all winter. The green and brown layered materials function as a compost pile, and the constant interplay between them heats up, then breaks down the entire pile, enriching the soil.

The bottom layer of cardboard in the garden lasagna blocks weeds from invading the new, appealing soil. What had been a used-up garden transforms into a sanctuary for your plants, with loose, fertile soil. This makes the next growing season easy and exciting.

If you “build” a lasagna garden in the late autumn or early winter, the magic starts right away. The four layers do their job: the cardboard prevents weed growth, the brown and green layers do their compost dance and decompose into the soil, and the top layer is ready to welcome seeds.

This lasagna garden should be fully decomposed and ready to plant by the following April or May. Autumn rain and winter moisture keep the layers moist. The organic layers require at least several months to break down.

If you put in a lasagna garden in spring or summer, you do so with the thought of immediate planting. Just dig small pockets into the top layer of the bed.

#7932. Montu: Martech Platforms & Data Manager (Braze)

Headquarters: Melbourne, Victoria, Australia
URL: https://www.montu.com.au

Company Description

Montu is Australia's largest healthtech business with a focus on alternative healthcare. Founded in 2019, it supports patients, doctors and pharmacies through its Alternaleaf clinic, offers accredited healthcare education to clinicians via its SAGED platform, and provides dispensing solutions to pharmacies across Australia through Leafio. Montu is also the founding member of Cannabis Council Australia, a not-for-profit advocacy body that advances legislative change across the healthcare landscape.

Guided by our Culture of Care, our mission is to make alternative healthcare more affordable and accessible for the millions who could benefit. This commitment was recently recognised at the Cannabiz Awards, where Montu took home Best Use of Technology for Alternaleaf's IDC and Distributor of the Year for Leafio.

Job Description

Sitting at the heart of CRM architecture and data engineering, you will support the technical platform function, directing the design, scaling, and integration of internal martech infrastructure across Montu Group’s ecosystems. Your remit spans platform architecture, data flow integrity, technical roadmaps, and the delivery of complex integrations to minimise engineering reliance.

In this role, you will build the robust technical foundation that powers scalable, automated, and hyper-personalised communications. You will support the configuration and governance of the martech stack, ensuring operational resilience and enabling advanced segmentation through sophisticated event and attribute schemas and seamless data orchestration. Hands on experience with Braze is essential.

Key Responsibilities:

Platform Architecture & Technical Strategy:

  • Integration Leadership: Lead the independent delivery of complex technical integrations (e.g., Zendesk, Litecard, Survicate) into the CRM environment to accelerate campaign delivery and business impact.
  • System Architecture: Drive strategic oversight of data architecture, managing pipelines and performing complex queries to power audience targeting and the definition of core business metrics.
  • Operational Resilience: Maintain high standards of implementation and QA across the tech stack, ensuring the reliability of data flows and the integrity of event-driven automation at scale.

Platform Ownership & Innovation:

  • Platform Strategy: Act as Braze platform owner, overseeing configuration, health, and performance. Drive adoption of advanced capabilities including dynamic personalisation, modular content, and journey automation.
  • Feature Enablement: Champion innovation by identifying, testing, and rolling out new platform features, working closely with Lifecycle, Product, and Data teams to maximise impact.
  • Channel Management: Lead CRM delivery across email, SMS, in-app messaging, content cards, landing pages, web forms, and mobile experiences.

Automation, Testing & Platform Integrity:

  • Lifecycle Orchestration: Develop and optimise patient lifecycle automations using custom events, attributes, and data triggers to deliver timely and relevant communications.
  • Issue Resolution: Diagnose and resolve logic, data, and platform issues that impact journey execution or personalisation accuracy. Act as a key escalation point for the team.
  • QA & Testing Standards: Establish and maintain robust testing frameworks, including UAT, journey validation, and ongoing performance monitoring.

Data Architecture & Personalisation: 

  • Data-Driven Targeting: Work with the Data team to activate behavioural and transactional signals to support intelligent segmentation and personalisation at scale.
  • Attribute & Event Management: Maintain a structured and scalable CRM data architecture, including user attributes, tags, and custom events.
  • Integration Oversight: Ensure reliability and integrity of data flows across systems (e.g. Segment, Hightouch, APIs), collaborating with engineering and product stakeholders where needed.

Platform Knowledge & Continual Development: 

  • Trends & Innovations: Stay abreast of emerging CRM trends, martech advancements, and patient engagement strategies. Translate insights into actionable improvements across CRM programs.
  • Operational Excellence: Identify and implement process enhancements to increase the efficiency, scalability, and resilience of CRM operations.

Team Enablement & Cross-Functional Collaboration:

  • Training & Capability Building: Upskill internal teams on platform features, logic frameworks, and best practice execution. Share documentation and promote technical excellence across the CRM team.
  • Stakeholder Alignment: Serve as the key CRM technical liaison across Product, Marketing, Tech, Data, and Compliance. Provide regular updates on platform performance, risks, and roadmaps.

Compliance, Data Governance & Sensitivity: 

  • Privacy and Compliance Management: Ensure all CRM initiatives adhere to the Privacy Act, SPAM Act, and other relevant data protection regulations. Follow best practices to safeguard patient data, and ensure all communications are compliant with regulations.
  • Legislation Awareness: Stay informed on changes to relevant legislation (such as updates from the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) and ensure all campaigns comply with updated guidelines. Communicate these updates to stakeholders as necessary.
  • Consent & Personal Data: Capture patient consent at key stages of the communication journey, and ensure data is used in accordance with privacy laws. Use this data to enhance profiling and personalise communication to better meet patient needs.

Qualifications

  • Education: Bachelor’s degree in Marketing Technology, Information Systems, Communications, or a related field.
  • Experience: 6+ years in CRM operations, marketing automation, or MarTech platform roles. Experience working in healthcare or other regulated industries is advantageous
  • Platform Expertise: Hands-on experience with CEPs such as Braze (mandatory), Salesforce Marketing Cloud, Adobe Campaign, or Iterable. Skilled in managing user attributes, custom events, Liquid personalisation, journey logic, content cards, and multichannel enablement
  • Technical Skills: Proficiency with scripting and markup languages including Liquid, HTML/CSS, JSON, and SQL. Comfortable navigating Braze’s developer tools, audience logic, and debugging environments. Experience with AI platforms such as Gemini and Claude.
  • System & Data Integration: Familiarity with CDPs (e.g. Segment, Hightouch), event/attribute schemas, and data flows that support lifecycle automation. Understanding of API interactions and cross-platform sync issues.
  • Channel Enablement: Strong understanding of how to optimise channels like email, SMS, in-app messaging, content cards, and webhooks for lifecycle communications
  • Issue Resolution & Troubleshooting: Experience diagnosing and resolving platform issues, campaign misfires, or automation bugs through structured testing and collaboration with technical teams.
  • Training & Collaboration: Ability to upskill others on platform features and champion best practices in naming conventions, tagging, and QA. Confident working cross-functionally with Product, Data, and CRM stakeholders
  • Governance & Compliance: Working knowledge of privacy legislation (Privacy Act, SPAM Act), data protection practices, consent frameworks, and unsubscribe handling.
  • Mindset: Curious, detail-oriented, and delivery-focused. Comfortable in fast-paced, agile environments with a passion for building infrastructure that supports scale, accuracy, and improved patient experiences.

#7931. Justice Thomas on the Second Amendment in "Sensitive Places"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v. Moore:

Maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places. Under Maryland law, an individual may not carry a firearm in public demonstrations, mass transit, places of amusement, healthcare facilities, locations that sell alcohol for onsite consumption, and tens of thousands of acres of state park and forest land. The Fourth Circuit upheld these restrictions against petitioners' Second Amendment challenge because it concluded that each law banned firearms in a "sensitive place."

I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari. Because each Maryland statute implicates a distinct historical tradition of firearm regulation, the breadth of petitioners' challenge would complicate our review. In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of States' authority to ban firearms in "sensitive places."

The Second Amendment recognizes the people's "inherent" right to keep and bear firearms, a right that admits of only historically grounded exceptions. Before and after the founding, it was well understood that individuals enjoyed a natural right to keep and bear arms, which included the right to carry firearms in public spaces for self-defense. The Constitution "codified [that] pre-existing right." The first generations after the founding recognized the breadth of the Second Amendment's "guarante[e]," and "those who sought to carry firearms publicly and peaceably in antebellum America were generally free to do so." Thus, when a State seeks to restrict the right to bear arms—including by limiting the places in which a law-abiding citizen may carry his firearm—the State must root its law in the Second Amendment's "historical understanding" by "demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation."

This Court has previously acknowledged a limited tradition of States' regulating the right to carry firearms in certain "sensitive places." In Bruen, we observed that early American legislatures sometimes prohibited weapons in "legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses." But, we emphasized that this tradition was narrow. "[T]he historical record yields relatively few 18th- and 19th-century 'sensitive places' where weapons were altogether prohibited." While "courts can use analogies to those historical regulations of 'sensitive places' to determine that modern regulations … are constitutionally permissible," "expanding the category of 'sensitive places' … to all places of public congregation … would eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense."

Nevertheless, States have seized on the idea of "sensitive places" to prohibit the peaceable carry of firearms in locations that bear little resemblance to legislatures, polling places, or courthouses. New Jersey, for example, prohibits firearms in at least 25 locations, including zoos, public libraries, casinos, and state-owned beaches. New York has designated 20 locations as "sensitive," ranging from "any place of worship" to "residential settings licensed … by the department of health." California's 29 gun-free spaces include "athletic facilit[ies]," "financial institution[s]," and any government-permitted "public gathering or special event." {Several other States ban firearms in many public places.} These restrictions stand on questionable historical ground. And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech—an affront to the right of "law-abiding citizens" to "carr[y] arms in public for" their "ordinary self-defense."

The lower courts have largely blessed these ahistorical ventures. The Fourth Circuit below upheld all but one of Maryland's locational restrictions. A now-vacated decision of the Third Circuit upheld many of New Jersey's "sensitive-place" laws. Courts of Appeals have also rejected challenges to specific locational restrictions in New York, California, and Hawaii.

I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions. In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.

#7929. 6 Native Alternatives to Butterfly Bush

Butterfly bush (Buddleja davidii, Zones 5–9) might seem like an easy choice for a pollinator bed, given the name, but is it the right shrub for your garden? There are a couple of reasons you might want to think twice and consider native butterfly bush alternatives instead.

Originally from Asia, butterfly bush is a prolific bloomer that attracts pollinators like no tomorrow. Unfortunately, it is also a prolific seeder, easily spreading past its intended area and potentially outcompeting other plants. Even after the shrub is removed, its seeds can remain viable in the soil for years until conditions are favorable for germination.

Butterfly bush is listed as an invasive plant by several state and regional invasive-plant organizations across the Southeast. Although some cultivars on the market are advertised as sterile or seedless, their fertility varies, and some can still produce small amounts of viable seed. While low-fertility cultivars can reduce the risk of spreading, butterfly bush also lacks an important benefit of many native plants: It does not serve as a host plant for native butterfly caterpillars.

The good news is that if you’re open to planting butterfly bush alternatives, there are plenty of beautiful flowering shrubs native to the Southeast that have both high visual appeal and benefits for native pollinators, including butterflies. Many also provide food and habitat beyond their flowering season. Here are just a few to get started:

Blooming in late spring to early summer, false indigo bush produces distinctive spikes of purple flowers that attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. A wonderful nectar source for long-tongued pollinators and a host plant for several butterflies, including the silver-spotted skipper and gray hairstreak, it offers benefits besides its gorgeous blooms. Its tolerance of a range of moisture conditions makes it a versatile option for sunny garden spaces.

Virginia sweetspire produces fragrant white flower spikes in late spring, followed by colorful foliage in fall. Its adaptability to moist soils makes it an especially useful shrub for rain gardens and other sites where drainage can be a challenge. A nectar source for many bees and butterflies, it is also reported as a host plant for the American holly azure butterfly in the coastal Southeast.

Its fragrant flowers attract butterflies, hummingbirds, and long-tongued bees. Blooming in late summer, when some other shrubs have finished flowering, summersweet offers an additional nectar source later in the growing season. Summersweet is also worth thinking about for gardens with consistently moist soil. Although it tolerates full sun, it generally needs more moisture in sunnier locations.

This deciduous native azalea brings soft pink to white flowers to woodland gardens in mid-spring, often before its foliage has fully emerged. An excellent nectar source for many pollinators, including hummingbirds and butterflies, pinxterbloom azalea is particularly well suited to partially shaded garden beds with acidic soil.

Spicebush blooms in early spring, producing small yellow flowers before its leaves emerge. Its early flowers also provide nectar for pollinators, while the bright red fall fruits on female plants, when a male plant is nearby for pollination, offer food for birds. A host plant for the spicebush swallowtail, this native shrub also brings pretty yellow foliage to the fall landscape.

Flame azalea earns its name from its showy flowers, which bloom in shades of yellow, orange, and red from late spring to early summer. A terrific general nectar source for many pollinators, particularly butterflies, this deciduous shrub adds striking seasonal color to woodland gardens and other partially shaded spaces.

If you’re only interested in the “butterfly” aspect of butterfly bush and not the “bush” aspect, choosing a great plant becomes even easier. There is an entire world of pollinator plants to explore, from host plants for the Southeast to nectar-rich native perennials and annuals. By incorporating both nectar plants for adults and host plants for caterpillars, you can create a garden that supports butterflies throughout their life cycle.

#7927. Spring Returns to Ezequiel’s Cottage Garden in Argentina

While many of our gardens are settling in for winter, Ezeiza, Argentina, is enjoying the last stretch of spring before summer arrives in December. Today we’re heading back to visit Ezequiel. We’ve followed his cottage garden through the seasons over the years, including another beautiful spring visit. After some difficult weather, he is back with another update as his garden fills with flowers ahead of summer.

I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North. In my country, following the harsh and troublesome “El Niño” weather phenomenon, the long-awaited and much-loved spring has finally arrived in my cottage garden in Ezeiza.

Plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere. Penstemons, salvias, irises, verbenas, dahlias, bulbines, daisies, and my lemon tree… Everything has begun to stir, grow, and grace us with beautiful blossoms, lovely scents, and fragrances.

Thank you, as always, for being there! And thank you for sharing in the joy of my garden.

From Argentina, sending you my best regards and a big hug.

A look into Ezequiel’s cottage garden in Ezeiza, Argentina.

‘Hot Lips’ salvia (Salvia microphylla ‘Hot Lips’, Zones 7–10) in bloom.

Louisiana iris (Iris × louisiana, Zones 4–9) showing off.

Purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea, Zones 3–9) are flowering next to the large sweep of lavender (Lavandula cvs., Zones 5–10) along the side of the driveway. I can practically smell the lavender looking at this photo!

This massive lantana (Lantana camara, Zones 8–11) stopped me in my tracks! Here in the North, we usually grow lantana as an annual because it isn’t winter hardy. Seeing what this tender perennial can become in a warmer climate is pretty incredible.

Bearded iris (Iris cvs., Zones 3–9), California poppy (Eschscholzia californica, Zones 8–10), and orange bulbine (Bulbine frutescens, Zones 9–11) make a colorful combination in this perennial bed.

Another view of the massive lantana, this time with a gorgeous specimen crimson bottlebrush (Callistemon citrinus, Zones 8–11) in full bloom.

Another view of the backyard. This photo has me wondering just how far it extends. I’m so curious about the layout of this garden—it seems like there’s something new to discover just about everywhere!

Thank you for bringing us back to your beautiful garden, Ezequiel! It’s always such a treat to see what’s growing in your corner of the world, especially while our seasons here in the North are moving in the opposite direction.

Have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!

#7926. How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

If you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers. Edible plants can bring striking foliage, flowers, fruit, and structure to a container, even when producing a harvest isn’t the primary goal.

As a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses. It’s no different when composing a container or a grouping of containers. For now, set aside flavor and look at their other sensory qualities: visual appeal, fragrance, texture, and even the sounds of foliage and seed heads moving in the wind.

Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell

Successful container design balances aesthetics with the growing needs of individual plants. Before exploring specific edimentals—plants valued for both their edible and ornamental qualities—consider a few practical guidelines.

Growing vegetables in containers demands certain conditions if you want a good harvest. But when appearance takes priority over production, you can make different choices. For instance, allowing lettuce and other leafy greens to bolt can introduce interesting flower stalks and seed heads, even though the leaves may become bitter and less desirable for eating.

Containers give you greater control over growing conditions, but plants still need the right light, moisture, and soil. Choose edible varieties that tend to be compact, dwarf, bush, or well-behaved vines or climbers.

It’s helpful to choose the largest container your budget and space will allow. Larger pots generally provide more room for roots and retain moisture longer, while smaller containers dry out more quickly and may require more frequent watering and feeding. Mixing container sizes also adds visual interest to a display. Whatever the size, make sure the container has adequate drainage.

One advantage of container gardening is the ability to tailor the soil to your plants’ needs. Start with a quality potting mix and choose plants with similar preferences for drainage, moisture, and soil acidity. This flexibility also lets you grow plants that might struggle in your native garden soil.

Because container plants depend on a limited volume of soil, they may need supplemental fertilizer as nutrients become depleted. Think about what you’re trying to encourage: Excess nitrogen, for example, can promote leafy growth at the expense of flowers or fruit. Choose a fertilizer appropriate for your plants, follow label directions, and consult your local nursery or Extension service for specific recommendations.

Mulch helps regulate soil temperature and retain moisture, even in containers. For open compositions where the soil surface is visible, use decorative materials such as small pine cones, shells, buckwheat hulls, or gravel. Leaf mold and finely shredded bark work well, too. Apply a shallow layer that allows water to pass through, and keep mulch away from plant crowns and stems.

Use what you have and think about growing your own. Many vegetables are quite easy to start from seed. Growing your own is both economical and a way to reduce the need for purchased transplants, especially when you use peat-free soil mixes. Choosing peat-free mixes can also help reduce demand for peat extracted from carbon-storing wetlands. Collect rainwater where permitted for an additional irrigation source. Avoid using untreated household gray water on edible crops. Incorporating perennials also extends the life of your displays. They can be combined with seasonal plants or relocated elsewhere in the garden when a container needs refreshing.

The ever-popular Thriller-Filler-Spiller container method holds its ground because of its snappy moniker and reliable formula. In this method, the thriller is the dramatic focal point; the filler is a bushy, mid-level plant or plants; and the spiller—wait for it—spills over the edge of the container. It’s an easy enough recipe that most people can create something attractive, but truthfully, many fail to think much about what they are combining, which results in the big-box special: a nondescript spiky grass towering over a showy fuchsia, with invasive creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia, Zones 3–9) trailing out.

We can do better. While perhaps less catchy, think about composing your container much like you might a landscape. Consider structure (the framework); form and habit (the shape); spatial orientation (how it reads visually—does the plant have a horizontal, vertical, or some other orientation?); visual texture (is the foliage fine, coarse, or medium?); and color (is it intense, receding, or something else?). Go beyond appearance and consider the full range of sensory experience: how plants move in the wind and what that sounds like, what they smell like, and how they feel when brushed up against.

Not every plant or combination will hit all the notes, so don’t stress. Focus on a few complementary qualities. Combine the plants in your container to create contrasts or enhance similarities. Look at leaf, bloom, and seed head form. The idea is to create layers—low, mid, and upper—and aim for three to five plants that play off each other’s traits within the container.

Are you trying to create something formal, informal, transitional, organic, or eclectic? Knowing how you want your container to read to the viewer can help you make choices about which edible plants may be a better addition to the mix.

When composing your containers, don’t forget to look beyond edimentals. Often the best containers mix edible plants with purely ornamental plants, such as leafy or flowering perennials and small shrubs. The juxtaposition of disparate plants usually determines a container’s success—different textures, colors, heights, and forms.

While incorporating disparate elements creates visual interest, it’s also important to give the eye somewhere to rest. A collection of pots filled with different plant combinations can feel jarring without repetition or quieter areas to balance the display.

A repeat may be exactly what it sounds like: using the same plant or using the same color, form, or texture across pots. Areas to pause are pots that may contain one uniform element—such as like plants, colors, or containers.

Another approach is to view the containers as individual components. Rather than composing containers with several different kinds of plants (including vegetables, of course), try grouping containers that each have one type of plant. This can be a powerful display akin to naturalistic block-style planting design.

Sometimes a container needs more. Perhaps it needs some staking for a vine, or simply a bit of additional texture. Incorporate natural materials such as pruned branches (dry or living), fallen branches covered in lichen, wild berry clusters, pine cones, grape or hop vines, dried elements such as grasses, or even small stumps.

And don’t neglect the value of seed heads—just because that kale bloom has now passed doesn’t necessarily mean you want to remove the plant; wait to see those prolific little yellow pods. And a radish gone to seed showcases its most redeeming feature: crunchy seed clusters that rattle in the wind!

By definition, a container is simply a receptacle for holding goods or objects, so feel free to think beyond the pots you find at the nursery. Salvaged and vintage items work well combined with more traditional terra-cotta pots. Take a high-low approach and use found items from your own home along with a special planter from a boutique garden center.

Don’t forget these irreverent options can also be repurposed in unexpected applications—that antique copper colander can go on to lead a new life as a hanging basket. Just make sure repurposed containers provide adequate drainage and are suitable for growing food if you plan to harvest from them.

One of the biggest benefits of working with containers is the opportunity to modify them by adding or removing plants to capture the best seasonal foliage. While many edibles are annuals that end their season late in the year, others produce seed heads or even a second flush after cutback.

Some common edible members of the carrot family (Apiaceae), including carrots (Daucus carota, biennial); parsnips (Pastinaca sativa, biennial); parsley (Petroselinum crispum, biennial); and celery and celeriac (Apium graveolens, biennial), produce flowers in their second growing season. Their delicate foliage and umbrella-shaped flower clusters add texture and attract pollinators. Deep-rooted crops such as carrots and parsnips need sufficiently deep containers, particularly if you plan to leave them in place for a second season.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera, Zones 4–9) isn’t a citrus fruit at all. This North American native tree produces large, greenish yellow, orange-like fruits with a distinctive, bumpy surface. Although the fruits aren’t considered edible, their unusual appearance and citrus-like fragrance make them wonderful decorative accessories for autumn container displays.

Another lesser-known edible is a well-known perennial: ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris, Zones 2–8). Its tightly coiled young fronds, known as fiddleheads, are harvested as a spring delicacy before unfurling into the familiar feathery foliage.

Lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, Zones 3–8) offers similarly beautiful emerging fronds for ornamental containers, but it should not be treated as an interchangeable edible. Many ferns contain potentially harmful compounds, so accurate identification is essential. Only properly identified ostrich fern fiddleheads should be eaten, and they must be thoroughly cooked. For more information, see the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s guide to fiddlehead safety. Of course, you can simply enjoy their fascinating emerging foliage up close in a container.

Vegetables that you may not have thought about embracing in your ornamental containers include okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, annual), with its large pods and hibiscus-like flowers; artichokes, such as ‘Purple Italian Globe’ (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus ‘Purple Italian Globe’, Zones 7–10), with dramatic silvery foliage and purple flower heads (use your largest container); cucamelon (Melothria scabra, annual), also called mouse melon, which resembles a tiny watermelon on a prolific climbing vine; and leafy greens of all sorts. Look out for the striking edible red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus, Zones 5–8), with the unpalatable common name, bloody dock—it’s a stunner. Its green leaves are marked with vivid red veins, and the young foliage is edible in moderation, although it contains oxalic acid.

More common edibles with uncommon traits include delicate currant tomatoes such as ‘Sweet Pea’ (Solanum pimpinellifolium ‘Sweet Pea’, annual) or compact tomatoes such as ‘Tiny Tim’ (Solanum lycopersicum ‘Tiny Tim’, annual).

Alpine strawberries (Fragaria vesca, Zones 4–9) come in a range of colors from white and pale yellow to pink and red, depending on the selection. These diminutive berries add character and spill over the edge of containers.

Peppers such as the teardrop ‘Biquinho Red’ (Capsicum chinense ‘Biquinho Red’, annual) are eye-catching and tolerant of many conditions. Compact blueberry (Vaccinium cvs., Zones 3–8) foliage glows red in the autumn, acting as a foil for its partners.

And there are so. Many. More. Whatever you’re interested in, you can find an edimental that will fill that niche.

Edible plants offer a broader palette that many gardeners and designers overlook—choosing them for containers broadens your range of plant materials and, most importantly, creates opportunities for delight and intrigue when used in unexpected ways.

They also make it possible to garden in small spaces or places where in-ground planting isn’t practical. Containers can be moved to improve growing conditions, rearranged to create a new focal point, or grouped to screen an unwanted view. They also let you accommodate plants that might struggle in your native soil or spread too aggressively in garden beds, such as mint (Mentha cvs., Zones 3–9) or sunchokes (Helianthus tuberosus, Zones 3–9). Just be sure to give vigorous plants enough room to grow.

In the eastern United States, ornamental kales and cabbages, paired with mums, are a common sight this time of year. While there is nothing inherently wrong with them, now you know you have more edimental options, so why not experiment with a wider range of edible plants? From colorful leafy greens to fruiting vines and impressive seed heads, there’s no shortage of possibilities for creating containers that look as interesting as the plants themselves.

Heather Tuckman is a garden designer and owner of Resilient Ground Design in southeastern Pennsylvania. She combines her background in horticulture, garden design, and psychology to create beautiful, ecologically thoughtful landscapes.

#7925. Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, new pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is important to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

It’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

Whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

#7923. GPOD on the Road: Shakespeare Garden in Evanston, Illinois

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

Earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

While wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

The garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

The garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

Jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

Last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

The Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.

#7922. Court Ordered Social Media Personality to Stop Posting About Teenagers He Accused as to Nolan Wells' Death

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The temporary restraining order was issued without giving the defendant, who posts as BoogieLowdown, a chance to respond.

The order was issued by a Mississippi state court Oct. 12; the case has just been removed to federal court, which will now consider the defendant's arguments against the injunction. Here's the key passage from the injunction, a temporary restraining order that was issued before the defendant could respond:

Here's the heart of plaintiffs' argument:

Defendants argue that the order isn't authorized by the Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law or by the Mississippi rules governing ordinary temporary restraining orders. But it also argues (I think correctly) that is an overbroad prior restraint that violates the First Amendment:

The order does not merely prohibit threats or harassment. It prohibits speech about the Plaintiffs, their families, and their lawyers—whether truthful or false, threatening or harmless, harassing or not. And it does so before that speech occurs. The Supreme Court has repeatedly condemned such prior restraints, particularly when imposed without notice or an opportunity to be heard.

The Court need not decide whether Mr. Hughes's commentary was fair, tasteful, or justified. The question is whether the law permits this order. It does not. The order should be dissolved, and the motion for a preliminary injunction denied….

A judicial order "forbidding certain communications when issued in advance of the time that such communications are to occur" is a prior restraint…. "Any system of prior restraints on communication bears a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity." Such restraints are unconstitutional "except in exceptional circumstances." .As the Supreme Court held in Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), {the party seeking to suppress speech} "carries a heavy burden of showing justification for the imposition of such a restraint." …

The remedy for false or injurious statements lies in "actions under libel laws providing for redress and punishment, and not in proceedings to restrain the publication." [But t]he October 12 Order … does not impose consequences for particular statements adjudicated unlawful. It prohibits Mr. Hughes from speaking about entire categories of people in the future. That is a prior restraint in its most direct form which is presumed unconstitutional….

Plaintiffs cannot justify the restraint merely by characterizing Mr. Hughes's commentary as malicious, coercive, or injurious. The Supreme Court rejected that reasoning in Keefe. There, the Court held that an individual's "interest in being free from public criticism of his business practices" did not justify an injunction against speech…. Plaintiffs may have remedies for unlawful conduct. But those remedies do not include an order forbidding Mr. Hughes from speaking about them at all….

Defendant also argues (again correctly, I think) that the order was unconstitutional because defendant wasn't given an opportunity to be heard before the order was entered:

The absence of notice presents a separate constitutional defect. In Carroll v. President & Commissioners of Princess Anne (1968), the Supreme Court set aside a short ex parte order restraining expression because of "a basic infirmity in the procedure by which it was obtained." The order "was issued ex parte, without notice to petitioners and without any effort, however informal, to invite or permit their participation in the proceedings."

There is a place in our jurisprudence for ex parte issuance, without notice, of temporary restraining orders of short duration; There is no place within the area of basic freedoms guaranteed by the First Amendment for such orders where no showing is made that it is impossible to serve or to notify the opposing parties and to give them an opportunity to participate.

The Court also rejected the suggestion that a later hearing could cure the problem. The availability of a subsequent opportunity to be heard "does not overcome the infirmity in the absence of a showing of justification for the ex parte nature of the proceedings."

The reason is straightforward. "The value of judicial decision-making … is substantially diluted where the process is ex parte, because the Court does not have available the fundamental instrument for judicial judgment: "an adversary proceeding in which both parties may participate." And where First Amendment freedoms are at stake, any order must be "couched in the narrowest terms that will accomplish the pin-pointed objective."

The October 12 Order fails both principles. It was entered without notice or an adversary hearing. It contains no finding that notifying Mr. Hughes was impossible. And far from identifying a narrow category of unlawful speech, it prohibits virtually any online commentary concerning the Plaintiffs, their families, or their counsel.

Carroll is directly controlling on the constitutional defect. An ex parte order restraining expression cannot stand without a showing that notice and participation were impossible. No such showing appears here….

#7921. "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

This short new article of mine has now been published in the Notre Dame Law Review. The Introduction:

There are many important big-picture questions about original meaning and the Free Speech, Free Press, Assembly, and Petition Clauses. This short Essay will leave those questions for others. Instead, it will offer as illustrations some specific, concrete questions—and, in some instances, answers—about original meaning and the freedom of expression. I hope these narrow illustrations can help us think about the broader questions.

From the table of contents, which should illustrate the subjects I cover:

I. Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals" B. Symbolic Expression C. Civil Liability II. Scant Evidence: Provoking a Riot III. Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels

Whether courts should shift the constitutional law of free expression to a more originalist footing is an important and difficult question. Perhaps it's a question that should be resolved entirely as a matter of constitutional theory—maybe such an approach is required by proper interpretive principles, or maybe it's forbidden by other principles (for instance, having to do with precedent).

But it's also possible that the answer may rest in part on how practically usable an originalist framework is likely to be. And to consider that, it's helpful to have in mind some practical questions. Some are already familiar, for instance questions related to damages liability in libel cases, obscenity law, and the like. This short Essay has aimed to help supplement those familiar examples with some others that haven't been much discussed; I hope others who think about the topic can find them useful.

I expect I'll post excerpts from the article in the coming days.

#7918. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options

Looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

Understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden

Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

Even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build new nests.

The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

#7917. Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

Hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:

In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

Arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

One of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

Another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something new to admire.

#7916. Pronouncing Law Latin

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A. Kelly (who is emeritus in the English Department). It's called "Lawyers' Latin: Loquenda ut Vulgus?," and here's the introduction (though all 14 pages of the article are much worth reading):

In "Rex v. Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A. P. Herbert's "Misleading Cases"), Mr. Wick, an advocate making his first appearance in the High Court, tries out his textbook Latin before the Lord Chief Justice. The young advocate, attempting to apply for a writ of certiorari, asks for "a rule of neesee of kairtiorahree." The Lord Chief Justice pretends not to understand this or any other of Mr. Wick's Latin phrases. When ultra vires is rendered ooltrah weerayze, the Court interrupts: "Stop! Listen, Mr. Wick. The two groups of sounds last formed by you have no meaning for me, and I order you not to make use of them again."

Although the unfortunate Mr. Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:

It is not for me at my time of life to learn a new language; it is not for the King's judges to remodel their diction according to the whims of pedagogues or the habits of the Junior Bar. The bitter conclusion is, Mr. Wick, that you must go away and learn to pronounce the Latin tongue correctly, according to the immemorial practice of your profession.

According to the juristic apophthegm, Loquendum ut vulgus, sentiendum ut docti, one should "speak like the common people but understand like the learned." When it comes to legal Latin, lawyers have observed the first part of this advice in various ways. Traditionally, Latin in England and other European countries has not been spoken uniformly but has been pronounced according to the sounds of the vernacular or lingua vulgaris of each region. Nowadays, however, most lawyers must be classed with the vulgus in never having learned Latin, and so they tend to avoid it whenever possible. But when an expression is unavoidable, they give it what they consider to be the "most common" pronunciation, or they imitate the commons in acting according to whim rather than according to rule. The result is what we might charitably call an eclectic or ad hoc approach—we hear, for example, ADD HOCK, ODD HAWK, ADD HOKE, ODD OAK, and so on.

Four different but internally consistent systems of Latin pronunciation have been used in England and America, each entirely "correct" and defensible in theory and in practice. The following analysis is concerned more with showing how the four methods have been adapted to English tongues than with reflecting how each would be spoken by a "native" or purist. My aim, after tracing the vagaries of Latin pronunciation, is to offer some practical recommendations to English-speaking lawyers using Latin phrases….

For the lawyer who occasionally uses Latin words or phrases, I recommend that all  expressions that have survived comfortably from an era when all Latin was pronounced in the English way—for example, et cetera—should continue to be pronounced as English, that is, in the English system of pronouncing Latin outlined above. But when Latin is cited as a foreign language, it should either be pronounced according to the system used by its author (if it is a literary citation) or according to any of the four systems outlined here that seems apt or convenient. Most often, no doubt, the system used will be the one learned in school.

But lawyers and legal educators should keep in mind the certainty of Herbert's Lord Chief Justice that such "hateful sounds" as "ooltrah weerayze" (for ultra vires) "will never proceed from the lips of an English judge, however many innocent boys are instructed to make them at school." Those who learned the Classical system need to be cautioned against trying to impose it upon all Latin expressions as if it were the only correct, or the most correct, way of pronouncing Latin. To do so would be to mistake the purpose of the scholars who resurrected it. It was intended only for the classics of the Golden Age of Latin, not for later Latin or for technical Latin terms or phrases brought into the various vernaculars in modern times

He labels the four methods "Classical (Ciceronian)," "Italian (Dantean)," "Continental (Chaucerian)," and "English (Shakespearean)," and discuss them further. He also cites a medieval source which I quite liked, at least with regard to pronunciation:

[T]he desire to appear wise among the foolish … is itself a kind of madness.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. #7915. Fall Color in Nancy’s Massachusetts Garden

Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

This is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

Sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy says she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what new plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

#7914. Shrubs Steal the Show in Bonnie’s Colorado Garden

Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie says the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:

Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

#7913. Episode 8: Best Ground Covers for Pollinators

On this episode of Super Cool Plants, we’re getting down and dirty to explore ground covers that do more than fill in the gaps. It’s true that the right low-growing plants can add texture and beauty to the bottom layer of your garden, but did you know that many creepers also provide valuable food and habitat for pollinators?

In fact, some of the earliest blooming plants for pollinators are those spring ground covers that many of us push on past at the nursery. From flowering carpets buzzing with bees to tough, adaptable plants that thrive where turfgrass struggles, we’ll dig into some super cool options for creating a living ground cover that supports pollinators and brings your garden to life.

#7912. Note to Second Circuit: Antisemitic Violence Shouldn't Get a Judicial Pass

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Torres v. Carlson, currently pending before the Second Circuit, is a case brought by two Columbia University janitors under the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (KKK Act).

According to their complaint, masked individuals from Columbia University's anti-Israel alliance, armed with hammers, knives, bolt cutters, chains, and zip ties, stormed Columbia's Hamilton Hall and confronted the two men. The janitors' refusal to yield drew the ire of the rioters, who then assaulted them, detained them, and slurred them as Jew-lovers, Jew-workers, and Zionists. The rioters proceeded to seize the building, break windows to chain the doors shut, barricaded themselves inside, and unfurled banners declaring an "Intifada."

Assuming the allegations are true, this seems like an open and shut case under the KKK Act, which the Supreme Court has described as reaching organized mob violence directed at a protected group and those perceived as standing with it. See Carpenters v. Scott, 463 U.S. 825 (1983).

Nevertheless, the district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. Covington & Burling has filed an amicus brief on behalf of Jon D. Michael of UCLA Law School, Matthew Segal of Tufts, with the Second Circuit, taking issue with the district court's decisions to:

(1) resolve at the pleading stage questions of motive in the defendants' favor, crediting the defendants' characterization of their own motives over the plaintiffs' allegations and dismissing explicit antisemitic epithets as irrelevant;

(2) treat supposed political motive as categorically negating discriminatory animus—disregarding both the mixed-motive framework that operates across federal antidiscrimination law and the settled principle that speech, even on political subjects, can evidence discriminatory intent; and,

(3) view Jewish disagreement about whether all anti-Zionism is inherently antisemitic as dispositive proof that the specific anti-Zionist rhetoric in this case was not plausibly antisemitic—a standard that conflicts with binding precedent, contradicts how courts apply antidiscrimination law to groups other than Jews, and improperly gives any individual Jew the power to veto discrimination claims by all other Jews.

As an aside, there are several federal court decisions arising out of post-October 7 protest activity that strike many, including me, as applying stricter standards to civil rights plaintiffs claiming anti-Jewish violations of civil rights laws than precedent suggests applies to other plaintiffs.

David Bernstein is the University Professor and the Executive Director of the Liberty & Law Center at the Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University.

#7910. 19-Year-Old Gets Probation (+ 6 Months Served) "After Firing over 20 Rounds, Shooting Boy Playing Basketball"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Darius Drew pleaded guilty on Aug. 10 to aggravated assault and carrying a pistol without a license. Although prosecutors asked Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro for a five-year prison term, she imposed a suspended 24-month sentence and placed him on probation under the Youth Rehabilitation Act, over the government's objection.

According to the government's evidence, Drew rode a Lime bike into an alley in the 700 block of Taylor Street NW on May 11.

Surveillance video showed him firing at a car parked in the alley. Seconds later, Drew fired toward a house near the alley in the 4100 block of Ninth Street NW, striking a boy who was playing basketball at a nearby recreation center. The boy suffered a leg injury.

Drew fired more than 20 rounds from two locations, prosecutors said….

From the opinion in U.S. v. Drew, released Monday by D.C. Superior Court Judge Jennifer A. Di Toro:

On August 10, 2026, Defendant Darius Drew entered a guilty plea to one count of Aggravated Assault and one count of Carrying a Pistol Without a License. Mr. Drew appeared before the Court for a sentencing hearing on November 13, 2026. At the hearing, the Court sentenced Mr. Drew to an aggregate term of incarceration of 24 months followed by 3 years of supervised release, with the execution of all but the 6 months he already served suspended in favor of 18 months of supervised probation.

In addition to the standard conditions of probation, the Court required that Mr. Drew participate in a comprehensive mental health assessment and treatment as deemed necessary by the Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency ("CSOSA"), undergo a substance abuse assessment and complete all treatment deemed necessary by CSOSA, and complete 90 hours of community service. He is required to register as a gun offender in the District of Columbia and remain registered for two years following the expiration of his period of probation. The Court entered an order requiring Mr. Drew to stay away from the location of the offense. During the period of probation, Mr. Drew is required to participate in either a GED program or vocational training and to maintain or seek employment. The Court also required Mr. Drew to appear before the Court for regularly-scheduled probation review hearings.

Because Mr. Drew was 19 years old at the time of this offense, he requested through counsel that he be sentenced under the Youth Rehabilitation Act ("YRA"), D.C. Code §§ 24-901 through 24-907. The Court now issues this "written statement on the record of the reasons for its determination" that Mr. Drew is eligible for and will be sentenced under the YRA, D.C. Code §24-903(c)(l). In deciding to sentence Mr. Drew pursuant to the YRA, the Court considered all of the factors set forth in D.C. Code §24-903(c)(2). Specifically, the Court evaluated:

For the foregoing reasons, the Court concludes that Mr. Drew should be treated as a youth offender for the purpose of sentencing. Accordingly, the Court granted a sentence pursuant to the YRA in this case.
